entry.title: The Only Time I Used Math at Work - and It wasn t What You Think
entry.summary:
My First “Simple” Task on the Team… Wasn’t So Simple position: sticky
before. The Layout Looked Straightforward A max‑width layout The requirement on paper: Make the menu sticky and make sure it stays aligned with the content. And for most screens, it did. Where Things Started to Break Ignoring large screens means ignoring real users. The Real Problem Match the content width To do that, I had to stop thinking in fixed pixel values.
At first glance it seemed simple: x = margin‑left + padding-left + width of the content column But — plot twist — x = sticky menu width Time for some real layout math. Breaking the Layout Down After inspecting and resizing the screen repeatedly, I discovered: 100vw = 2y + 2P + B
Where: 100vw = viewport width And the sticky menu width: x = y + C1 + P
Where C1 was the fixed width of the content section itself. { x = y + C1 + P 100vw = 2y + 2P + B }
Solve for y: y = (100vw - 2P - B) / 2
Plug it into the first equation: x = ((100vw - P - B) / 2) + C1 + P
And that gave me the responsive width I needed. The Final CSS @media (min-width: 1439px) { .sticky { width: calc(((100vw - 1202px - 8px) / 2) + 794px + 4px); } }
Final Thoughts 1. Web development has to consider big screens too.
Mobile (of course) But high‑resolution monitors are everywhere now. 2. Math hides quietly in everyday front‑end work.
Just enough to make layouts behave. Sometimes being a developer means doing a little math… And honestly, that’s kind of perfect.

entry.title: Data Science - Time Series Forecasting - Complete Tutorial
entry.summary:
Data Science - Time Series Forecasting - Complete Tutorial
In this tutorial, we will delve into Time Series Forecasting, a critical component in the field of Data Science & Analytics. Perfect for intermediate developers, this guide will walk you through understanding, constructing, and predicting time series data using Python. Time Series Forecasting is used to predict future values based on previously observed values. It's applicable in various domains like finance for stock prices prediction, weather forecasting, and more. Intermediate Python knowledge Basic understanding of statistical concepts Familiarity with pandas and NumPy libraries import numpy as np import pandas as pd from statsmodels.tsa.arima_model import ARIMA
Load your time series data. data = pd.read_csv('your_time_series_data.csv', parse_dates=['Date'], index_col='Date') print(data.head())
Identify trends, seasonality, and noise. from pandas.plotting import autocorrelation_plot autocorrelation_plot(data['Your_Column'])
Select and configure the ARIMA model. model = ARIMA(data['Your_Column'], order=(5,1,0)) model_fit = model.fit(disp=0) print(model_fit.summary())
Split the data into training and test sets to evaluate the model's performance. Forecast future values. forecast = model_fit.forecast(steps=5) print(forecast)
Always perform EDA before model selection. Tune your model's parameters for better accuracy. Consider using additional models like LSTM for complex time series data. Time Series Forecasting is a powerful technique for predictive analytics. With this tutorial, you should now be able to model and forecast time series data effectively. Dive into your data and start forecasting!
